differences.title: 1. COMMUNICATION PROTOCOL
differences.leftDesc: Leverages HTTP/2's binary framing for multiplexing and header compression, reducing latency and overhead significantly compared to text-based HTTP/1.1.
differences.rightDesc: Relies on HTTP/1.1, which is text-based and can suffer from head-of-line blocking, requiring multiple connections or workarounds for efficiency.

differences.title: 2. DATA FORMAT
differences.leftDesc: Uses Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) for efficient, compact, and strongly-typed serialization, enforcing schema adherence and reducing payload size.
differences.rightDesc: Typically uses JSON or XML, which are human-readable but less efficient in size and parsing speed, offering flexibility but less strict typing.

differences.title: 3. CONTRACT DEFINITION
differences.leftDesc: Requires a formal .proto file to define services and messages, acting as a strong contract ensuring client-server compatibility.
differences.rightDesc: Often relies on documentation (e.g., OpenAPI) or implicit agreements, making contract enforcement less robust and prone to runtime errors.

differences.title: 4. PERFORMANCE
differences.leftDesc: Optimized for low latency and high performance due to binary serialization, efficient transport, and HTTP/2 capabilities, ideal for microservices.
differences.rightDesc: Performance can be limited by text parsing, network overhead, and HTTP/1.1 limitations, though improvements exist with HTTP/2 and JSON optimizations.

differences.title: 5. STREAMING
differences.leftDesc: Natively supports bidirectional streaming, enabling real-time, low-latency communication for complex scenarios like chat or live data feeds.
differences.rightDesc: Primarily uses a request-response model. Streaming is often simulated via techniques like WebSockets or Server-Sent Events, adding complexity.

differences.title: 6. TOOLING & ECOSYSTEM
differences.leftDesc: Relies heavily on code generation from .proto files for clients and servers, offering strong type safety but requiring a build step.
differences.rightDesc: Extremely mature ecosystem, with ubiquitous browser support and a vast array of libraries and tools for almost any language.

differences.title: 7. BROWSER SUPPORT
differences.leftDesc: Direct browser support for gRPC is limited. Typically requires a proxy like gRPC-Web to translate requests for compatibility.
differences.rightDesc: Directly supported by all modern web browsers, making it the de facto standard for client-to-server web communication.
